module_title: Sorting, Grading, and Pricing Your Items

lessons.title: Sorting Clothes by Quality: First Grade, Second Grade, and Rags
lessons.body:
When your bale of okrika arrives, the first thing you must do is sort everything into three piles: First Grade, Second Grade, and Rags. This is the foundation of your profit. First Grade items are like newâno stains, no holes, no fading, all buttons and zips working. These are your money-makers. Second Grade has minor flaws: a small stain that might wash out, a loose thread, slight fading, but still wearable. Rags are torn, heavily stained, or missing partsâthese you can sell to tailors or rag pickers for a small amount.

Start by spreading everything on a clean tarpaulin or mat in a well-lit area. Work in natural daylight if possible, because artificial light can hide stains. Pick up each item, check the front, back, inside, seams, underarms, and crotch area. For trousers, check the knees and pockets. For dresses, check the hem and zips. A simple rule: if you would not wear it to a wedding or an interview, it is not First Grade.

Use a simple grading system: A for First Grade, B for Second Grade, C for Rags. You can mark this with a small tag or sticker, or just separate them into different bags. Keep a count as you goâthis helps with record-keeping later. For example, from a 50kg bale costing 150,000 Naira, you might get 30% First Grade, 50% Second Grade, and 20% Rags. That means 15kg of First Grade, 25kg of Second Grade, and 10kg of Rags. Knowing these percentages helps you price your bale correctly.

Be ruthless with your sorting. It is better to under-grade than over-grade. A customer who buys a Second Grade item thinking it is First Grade will not return. Your reputation is built on honesty. Also, remember that some items can be upgraded: a Second Grade shirt with a missing button becomes First Grade after you sew on a matching button. Keep a small sewing kit handyâneedle, thread, scissors, and spare buttons. A 30-minute repair can double the price of an item.

Finally, store your sorted piles separately. Use clean sacks or boxes labeled A, B, and C. Keep them dry and away from direct sunlight to prevent damage. This simple sorting process will save you hours later and ensure you get the best price for every item.

lessons.title: Identifying Branded and Vintage Items for Higher Profit
lessons.body:
Not all okrika is equal. Some items are worth 10 times more than others because of the brand name or vintage appeal. Your job is to spot these gems before you price them. Branded items include known labels like Nike, Adidas, Zara, H&M, Levi's, Gucci, and local favorites like Ankara or Dashiki from reputable designers. Vintage items are older pieces, often from the 70s, 80s, or 90s, that have a unique style and quality.

How do you identify a brand? Check the label inside the collar or waistband. Look for the brand name, logo, and sometimes a size and country of origin. Be careful: some fakes exist. A real Nike will have a consistent logo, good stitching, and a quality feel. A fake will have crooked stitching, misspelled words, or a cheap label. For vintage, look for details like metal zips, single-stitch seams, and old-fashioned sizing (e.g., size 42 instead of L). Also, check for union labels or old care tags.

Once you find a branded or vintage item, set it aside in a special 'Premium' pile. These items should not be mixed with the general stock. For example, a vintage Levi's 501 jeans in good condition can sell for 15,000 to 25,000 Naira, while a regular jeans might sell for 3,000 Naira. A Nike hoodie can fetch 8,000 Naira, while a no-name hoodie goes for 2,500 Naira. The difference is huge.

To learn brands, spend time online. Follow thrift and vintage sellers on Instagram and TikTok. Use Google Lens to search for a logo you don't recognize. Join Facebook groups for okrika sellers where people share tips. Also, visit high-end thrift stores in your city and see what they price high. Ask questions. The more you know, the more money you make.

When you find a premium item, clean it carefully. Hand wash or dry clean if needed. Present it wellâuse a mannequin or hang it prominently in your shop. Take clear photos for online sales. Mention the brand and vintage status in your description. This attracts buyers who are willing to pay more. Remember, one premium item can pay for a whole bale, so train your eye to spot them.

lessons.title: Setting Prices Based on Condition, Brand, and Demand
lessons.body:
Pricing is both an art and a science. You must consider three main factors: condition, brand, and demand. Condition is the most important. A First Grade item can be priced at 3 to 5 times your cost per item, while Second Grade should be 1.5 to 2 times cost, and Rags sold in bulk. For example, if your average cost per item from a bale is 500 Naira, First Grade could sell for 2,000 to 2,500 Naira, Second Grade for 800 to 1,000 Naira, and Rags for 100 Naira per kg.

Brand adds value. A branded item in First Grade can be priced 20-50% higher than a similar non-branded item. For instance, a plain shirt might sell for 1,500 Naira, but a Zara shirt in the same condition can sell for 2,500 Naira. Vintage items can be priced even higher, often 3-5 times the base price. Do your research: check online marketplaces like Jumia, Konga, or Facebook Marketplace to see what similar items are selling for.

Demand is about what your customers want. In many African markets, certain items are always in demand: jeans, t-shirts, dresses, and children's clothes. Seasonal demand also matters: raincoats during rainy season, sweaters during harmattan. If you have an item that is in high demand, you can price it slightly higher. But be careful not to overpriceâcustomers will walk away. A good strategy is to start with a price 10-20% above your target, so you have room to negotiate.

Also consider your location. Prices in a busy market like Balogun in Lagos will be different from a small town in Ghana. Talk to other sellers, observe what customers are buying, and adjust. Keep a notebook or use a simple app like Excel or Google Sheets to track your prices and sales. After a month, you will see which prices work and which don't.

Finally, don't be afraid to change prices. If an item is not selling after two weeks, reduce the price by 10-20%. If it sells quickly, you might have underpriced itâraise the price for similar items next time. Pricing is a skill you build with experience.

lessons.title: Pricing Strategies for Quick Turnover vs. High Margins
lessons.body:
You have two main pricing strategies: quick turnover (sell fast, lower profit per item) and high margins (sell slow, higher profit per item). Your choice depends on your cash flow needs, storage space, and customer base. Quick turnover is good if you need cash quickly to buy more bales or if you have limited storage. High margins work if you have a loyal customer base that values quality and you can afford to wait.

For quick turnover, price your items 20-30% lower than competitors. For example, if a shirt normally sells for 2,000 Naira, price it at 1,500 Naira. This attracts bargain hunters and moves stock fast. You might sell 50 items a day at 1,500 Naira, making 75,000 Naira, but your profit per item is small. This strategy works well in busy markets with high foot traffic. You can also offer 'buy 2 get 1 free' or '3 for 5,000 Naira' to encourage bulk buying.

For high margins, focus on quality and presentation. Price your First Grade and branded items higher. For instance, a vintage dress might be priced at 10,000 Naira instead of 5,000 Naira. You might sell only 5 items a day, but each sale gives you a big profit. This works if you have a nicheâlike vintage clothing or plus-size fashionâand you market to the right audience. Use social media to showcase your premium items. Create a loyal following by offering excellent customer service and unique pieces.

You can also mix both strategies. Have a 'bargain bin' for quick turnover of Second Grade and Rags, and a 'premium rack' for high-margin items. This way, you attract all types of customers. For example, a customer comes for a cheap t-shirt, sees a beautiful vintage jacket, and buys both. The cheap item brings them in, the premium item makes your profit.

Track your sales weekly. If you find that you are selling out of certain items too fast, you are underpricing. If items sit for months, you are overpricing. Adjust accordingly. Remember, cash flow is king. Even if you make high margins, if you don't sell, you can't pay rent or buy new stock. Find the balance that works for your business.

lessons.title: Creating Bundle Deals and Discounts to Move Slow Items
lessons.body:
Every okrika seller has slow-moving itemsâthose that have been on the rack for weeks or months. Instead of letting them gather dust, use bundle deals and discounts to move them. Bundling means grouping several items together and selling them at a lower combined price. For example, if you have 10 shirts that are not selling at 1,000 Naira each, offer a '5 shirts for 4,000 Naira' deal. That's 800 Naira per shirt, but you sell 5 at once. Customers love a bargain, and you clear stock.

Another bundle idea: create themed packages. For children's clothes, offer '10 pieces for 3,000 Naira'. For ladies' tops, '3 for 2,500 Naira'. You can also bundle by size: 'All size M shirts, 4 for 3,000 Naira'. This makes it easy for customers to buy multiple items. Make sure the bundle price is lower than the individual total, but still gives you a profit. Calculate your cost per item and ensure the bundle price covers it plus a small margin.

Discounts are another tool. Offer a percentage off for bulk buys: 'Buy 3, get 10% off' or 'Buy 5, get 20% off'. You can also have a 'Happy Hour' discountâsay, every Wednesday from 2-4 PM, everything is 20% off. This creates urgency and brings in customers during slow hours. For online sales, use promo codes like 'OKRIKA10' for 10% off. Announce these deals on WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook.

For very slow items, consider a 'clearance sale' at the end of the month. Price everything in a specific bin at 500 Naira or 1,000 Naira, regardless of original price. This generates excitement and brings people to your shop. They might buy other items too. Even if you break even or make a small loss on those items, you free up space for new stock that will sell better.

Always communicate the value. Tell customers why you are discountingâ'End of season sale' or 'Making room for new arrivals'. This makes them feel they are getting a deal, not buying rejected goods. Also, use bundles to upsell: when a customer buys one item, suggest a bundle. 'This shirt is 1,500 Naira, but if you add two more, you get all three for 4,000 Naira.' Many will take the offer. This increases your average sale and moves stock faster.

lessons.title: Record-Keeping for Stock and Sales
lessons.body:
If you don't keep records, you are running a hobby, not a business. Record-keeping helps you know what you have, what you sold, and what you earned. Start simple: get a notebook and pen, or use a free app like Excel, Google Sheets, or a simple inventory app on your phone. The key is to record every item you buy and every item you sell.

For stock, create a list with columns: Date, Item Description, Grade (A, B, C), Cost Price, Selling Price, and Quantity. When you buy a bale, record the total cost and the number of items you sorted into each grade. For example, on 1st January, you bought a bale for 150,000 Naira and got 100 First Grade, 150 Second Grade, and 50 Rags. This gives you an average cost per item: 150,000 / 300 = 500 Naira per item. But you can allocate costs differently: First Grade might carry more of the cost because they sell higher. A simple method is to assign 70% of the bale cost to First Grade, 25% to Second Grade, and 5% to Rags. So First Grade cost per item = (0.7 * 150,000) / 100 = 1,050 Naira. Second Grade = (0.25 * 150,000) / 150 = 250 Naira. Rags = (0.05 * 150,000) / 50 = 150 Naira per item. This helps you set prices accurately.

For sales, record every sale: Date, Item, Quantity, Selling Price, Total. At the end of each day, total your sales. At the end of the week, calculate your profit: Total Sales - Total Cost of Items Sold. Also track expenses like rent, transport, and your own time. This shows if you are truly making a profit.

Use a simple stock card for each item or a spreadsheet. If you have many items, use a numbering system: write a number on a tag and attach it to the item. In your record book, write that number with the details. When sold, mark it as sold. This prevents theft and helps you know what is missing. For online sellers, keep a record of orders, customer names, and delivery status.

Finally, review your records monthly. Identify your best-selling items, your most profitable grades, and your slow movers. This data guides your future purchases. For example, if you see that First Grade jeans sell out every month, buy more bales with jeans. If Rags are not selling, find a new buyer or donate them. Good records turn a small okrika business into a growing enterprise.

quiz.q: What are the three grades used when sorting okrika clothes?
options: A) First Grade, Second Grade, Rags
quiz.explanation: The lesson explicitly states that clothes are sorted into First Grade, Second Grade, and Rags.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of a First Grade item?
options: A) Minor stain that might wash out
B) All buttons and zips working
C) Small hole in the seam
quiz.explanation: First Grade items are like new, with no stains, holes, fading, and all buttons and zips working.

quiz.q: Why is it important to sort clothes in natural daylight?
options: B) Artificial light can hide stains
quiz.explanation: Natural daylight helps you see stains and flaws that artificial light might hide.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when you find a Second Grade item with a missing button?
options: A) Throw it in the rags pile
B) Sell it as First Grade without fixing
C) Sew on a matching button to upgrade it
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests keeping a sewing kit to repair items and upgrade them to First Grade.

quiz.q: How can you calculate the average cost per item from a bale?
options: A) Divide total bale cost by total number of items sorted
B) Divide total bale cost by number of First Grade items
C) Multiply total bale cost by 0.5
quiz.explanation: Average cost per item is total bale cost divided by the total number of items sorted from that bale.

quiz.q: Which brand is mentioned as an example of a branded item?
quiz.explanation: Nike is listed as a known brand that can fetch higher prices.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a branded item might be fake?
options: B) Misspelled words on the label
quiz.explanation: Fake items often have misspelled words or poor stitching.

quiz.q: What is a good way to learn about brands and vintage items?
options: B) Follow thrift sellers on social media
quiz.explanation: Following thrift and vintage sellers online helps you learn to identify valuable items.

quiz.q: How much more can a vintage Levi's 501 jeans sell for compared to a regular jeans, according to the lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a vintage Levi's 501 can sell for 15,000 to 25,000 Naira, while a regular jeans might sell for 3,000 Naira, which is 5 to 8 times more.

quiz.q: What should you do with premium items after identifying them?
options: A) Mix them with general stock
B) Set them aside in a special pile
quiz.explanation: Premium items should be kept separate and priced higher.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when setting prices?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that condition is the most important factor in pricing.

quiz.q: If your average cost per item is 500 Naira, what is a suggested price range for First Grade items?
quiz.explanation: First Grade items can be priced at 3 to 5 times cost, so 1,500 to 2,500 Naira.

quiz.q: How much higher can a branded item be priced compared to a non-branded item of similar condition?
quiz.explanation: Branded items can be priced 20-50% higher than similar non-branded items.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy to allow room for negotiation?
options: A) Start with a price 10-20% above your target
B) Start with a price 50% above
quiz.explanation: Starting 10-20% above your target gives you room to negotiate down to your desired price.

quiz.q: What should you do if an item is not selling after two weeks?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests reducing the price by 10-20% if an item is not selling after two weeks.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of quick turnover pricing strategy?
quiz.explanation: Quick turnover focuses on selling many items quickly, even with lower profit per item.

quiz.q: Which pricing strategy is best if you have limited storage space?
quiz.explanation: Quick turnover moves stock fast, freeing up storage space.

quiz.q: What is an example of a bundle deal?
quiz.explanation: A bundle deal groups multiple items for a combined lower price, like 5 shirts for 4,000 Naira.

quiz.q: What is a 'clearance sale'?
options: A) Selling everything at original price
B) Pricing slow items at a very low fixed price
quiz.explanation: A clearance sale prices slow-moving items at a low fixed price to clear stock quickly.

quiz.q: How can you create urgency for a discount?
options: A) Offer it only on certain days or hours
B) Always have the same discount
quiz.explanation: Limited-time discounts, like Happy Hour, create urgency and bring in customers.

quiz.q: Why is record-keeping important for an okrika business?
options: B) To know what you have and what you earn
quiz.explanation: Record-keeping helps you track stock, sales, and profit, turning a hobby into a business.

quiz.q: What columns should a simple stock record include?
options: A) Date, Item, Grade, Cost Price, Selling Price, Quantity
C) Customer name and phone number
quiz.explanation: The lesson lists these columns for effective stock recording.

quiz.q: If a bale costs 150,000 Naira and yields 100 First Grade, 150 Second Grade, and 50 Rags, what is the average cost per item?
quiz.explanation: Total items = 300, so 150,000 / 300 = 500 Naira per item.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using a numbering system for items?
options: A) It prevents theft and helps track inventory
B) It makes items more expensive
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Numbering items helps you track what you have, what is sold, and what is missing.

quiz.q: How often should you review your records to identify trends?
quiz.explanation: Monthly review helps you identify best-sellers and slow movers to guide future purchases.

quiz.q: What should you do with Rags that are not selling?
options: B) Find a new buyer or donate
C) Sell them as First Grade
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests finding a new buyer or donating rags if they are not selling.

quiz.q: Which of these is a vintage detail to look for?
quiz.explanation: Vintage items often have metal zips and single-stitch seams.

quiz.q: What is a good way to price a premium item?
quiz.explanation: Vintage and premium items can be priced 3-5 times the base price.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if you sell out of an item too quickly?
options: A) Raise the price for similar items next time
D) Buy more at any cost
quiz.explanation: Selling out too fast may mean you underpriced; raise prices for similar items in the future.

quiz.q: What is a mixed pricing strategy?
options: C) Having a bargain bin and a premium rack
quiz.explanation: A mixed strategy uses both quick turnover for some items and high margins for others.
